prompt:
TASK: READ ONE INSTRUMENT ENTRY AND ANSWER THREE QUESTIONS

Below is one entry from the specification of a web measurement instrument. The instrument checks
public websites of U.S. federal statistical agencies and reports, per agency, whether each check
passed or failed. The entry states the check's question, the behavior a ready publisher is
expected to show (with verbatim quotes from the sources it cites), the test the instrument runs,
and what a pass and a fail claim.

Terms the project defines once for every entry (they are not undefined): SI client (SI system): a system that finds, reads and uses data on its own, such as an answer engine, an agent or a retrieval pipeline; the project's term for what is elsewhere called an AI system; data page: an agency's own web page for one data product, the page the harness measures (also 'product page' in rule code); harness: this project's scanner: an identified, robots-compliant HTTP client that fetches the pages and records what it met; cycle of record: the scan whose results the published grid is built from (here scan_2026-10-07_composite_d); recorded location: an address for an agency's API, terms, changelog or inventory that the harness was given, read from the agency's own pages or seeded from a named source; error / not measured: the harness could not observe: an access denial, its own robots compliance, an absence it could not confirm, or a server or network error; never a fail; leg: one check as the harness runs it, named by its indicator code (A1, D4); each leg has one rule, and the codes in a test field name other legs whose fetches this one reuses; rule / branch: the versioned code that turns observations into a verdict; a branch is one way the rule can reach a verdict, with its own reason text; Observation: one recorded fetch (request, response, parsed content) that a rule judges; surface: the page a verdict is about: a data page, or for site-level checks the agency's home host; body: the agency, as the harness's records name it; complete search: an absence is reported as a fail only when every candidate location was observed and every named source searched; otherwise the verdict is error (DN-012); seed source: a named place a recorded location came from: the agency's own developer page, catalog.data.gov, api.data.gov, this repository's citations, or a model's knowledge, each recorded per location; params.*: a named parameter in the harness's configuration file (assessment/harness/scan/params.yaml); its value is stated where it matters

Answer from the entry alone. For question 1, the QUOTED SOURCE PASSAGES are the only evidence of
what the sources say; do not use what you know of them from elsewhere.

1. Does the EXPECTED BEHAVIOR come from the cited sources and not from the writer? Answer "yes"
   if every requirement the expected-behavior text attributes to a source is supported by a
   quoted passage, and any part no source defines is said plainly to be undefined or the
   project's own. Answer "no" if it states as a source's requirement something the passages do
   not contain; name it.
2. Could a reader who knows the agency misread a FAIL on this check as a claim the test did not
   make? Answer "yes" if the CLAIMS leave such a misreading open (name it), "no" if they close it.
3. Is any term in the entry undefined for a technically literate reader new to this project?
   Answer "yes" and list the terms, or "no".

Return ONLY a JSON object, with no prose before or after it and no code fence:
{"q1": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "why": "..."}, "q2": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "why": "..."}, "q3": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "terms": ["..."], "why": "..."}}

ENTRY
CHECK: A11-declared (RULE-A11-declared-v2) — a declaration

QUESTION:
What does the host declare about crawler access to the data page, in both places a declaration can live (robots.txt and the page's robots meta tag)? A declaration is the publisher's stated policy; it is half of the question whether crawlers are let in, and the half that can be read from outside.
Established by: rfc-9309-robots-exclusion-protocol (§1; §2.2); cloudflare-ai-crawl-control-manage-crawlers (Manage AI crawlers (allow or block per crawler))

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR:
This is a declaration check: it states what the host declares, and its expected behavior is the declaration's meaning. RFC 9309: the rules are not a form of access authorization (§1, quoted), and a robots.txt the server reports as unavailable lets the crawler access any resources (§2.3.1.3, quoted). Google: the robots meta tag's noindex rule applies to search engine crawlers, and such settings can be followed only if crawlers are allowed to access the pages that carry them (quoted). OpenAI: disallowing GPTBot means content should not be used in training, and allowing OAI-SearchBot helps a site appear in search results (quoted). Anthropic: restricting ClaudeBot signals exclusion from model training (quoted). Reading a training opt-out as a restriction on answers is not supported by these sources.
Cited sources: rfc-9309-robots-exclusion-protocol (§1; §2.3.1.3); https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag (Using the robots meta tag); openai-crawlers-bots (GPTBot; OAI-SearchBot); anthropic-crawler-support-article (ClaudeBot)

QUOTED SOURCE PASSAGES (verbatim):
- [rfc-9309-robots-exclusion-protocol] "then the crawler MAY access any resources on the server."
- [https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag] "rule applies to search engine crawlers"
- [openai-crawlers-bots] "Disallowing GPTBot indicates a site's content should not be used in training generative AI foundation models."
- [rfc-9309-robots-exclusion-protocol] "These rules are not a form of access authorization."
- [https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag] "these settings can be read and followed only if crawlers are allowed to access the pages that include these settings"
- [openai-crawlers-bots] "To help ensure your site appears in search results, we recommend allowing OAI-SearchBot in your site's robots.txt file"
- [anthropic-crawler-support-article] "it signals that the site's future materials should be excluded from our AI model training"
- [cloudflare-ai-crawl-control-manage-crawlers] "For each AI crawler, you can choose to allow or block access."

TEST:
Client: the harness's identified client
Request: GET /robots.txt; read the data page's robots meta tags
Reads: per-token verdicts for the same eight tokens as A4; restricting meta-robots tokens
Decision rule:
- fail: `nothing is DECLARED: no robots.txt is served`
- fail: `robots.txt DISALLOWS the product path for {k} of {n} AI-crawler user agents`
- fail: `robots.txt permits every AI crawler but the product page's meta-robots directives restrict it`
- pass: `both declared-layer sources permit`
Parameters: params.a4_crawlers.user_agents (the A4 list)
Is it the recognized way to measure the behavior: Parsing robots.txt per RFC 9309 and reading the meta tag as Google defines it are the declarations' own semantics.

BRANCHES (each verdict branch of the rule; the behavior it rewards or penalizes; its source):
- pass_both_permit (pass): both declarations permit every listed token Source: rfc-9309-robots-exclusion-protocol (§2.2).
- fail_nothing_declared (fail): penalizes no robots.txt, which RFC 9309 reads as permitting everything Source: rfc-9309-robots-exclusion-protocol (§2.3.1.3 (contradicts the branch)).
- fail_token_disallowed (fail): penalizes a training opt-out as if it were a refusal of access Source: openai-crawlers-bots (GPTBot (contradicts the branch)).
- fail_meta_restricts (fail): the page declares noindex or a similar restriction Source: https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag (Using the robots meta tag).

CLAIMS:
A pass claims: Both the host's robots.txt and the page's robots meta tags, as declared, permit each of the eight listed crawler tokens.
A fail claims: One of three things, named in the reason: the robots.txt disallows a listed token (for five of the eight tokens that is a training opt-out, not a restriction on answers); the page's robots meta tags restrict it; or no robots.txt is served, which declares no restriction at all and under the standard permits every crawler. A fail is therefore not a claim that the agency declared a policy restricting crawler access. It is about declared policy only, not about whether any crawler is served or refused.
Neither claims: Nothing about enforcement (A12) or observed crawler traffic (agency-enabled).

CONFOUNDS:
- the same token-list and absent-file problems as A4. Distinguished: no.
